newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says close to eliminating measles.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says close to eliminating measles.

text.p: U.S. measles rates remained near all-time lows last year but federal health officials on Thursday stressed the need for children to obtain the recommended two doses of vaccine if the disease is to be eliminated.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said there were 488 measles cases reported in 1996. There were 301 cases in 1995, the lowest number in one year since measles became a notifiable disease in 1912.
"Elimination of measles in the United States is achievable," the CDC said.
Measles cases were down sharply from 1990, when 27,786 were reported during the peak of a resurgence. More than two-thirds of last year's cases involved importation from other countries.
"We won't be able to achieve eradication in the United States until there is worldwide eradication," Dr. Ann Thomas of the CDC's National Immunization Program said.
Health officials stressed the need for children to get one dose of measles-mumps-rubella vaccine at age 12 to 15 months and a second dose between the ages of 4 and 6 or between 11 and 12.

"Most schoolchildren have had a first dose of measles vaccine but the vaccine works on essentially 95 percent of people," Thomas said. "By advocating that children get a second dose by the time they go to school, that will take care of the remaining five percent who it didn't work on the first time."
"For 1996, two-thirds of the cases that we had were traced to international importation," Thomas said.

She played down the increase in cases from 1995 to 1996. "That fluctuation is not a major concern," she said. "In the last four years in a row we've had less than a thousand. And in three of those four years there were less than 500.
"It's a pretty remarkable achievement, actually, to still have only 500 cases," Thomas said.
